data.title: The Book of Precious Records – ibn Rusta on Svatopluk
data.excerpt: The Book of Precious Records was written at the beginning of the 10th century, after 903, by the Arab-Persian geographer ibn Rusta. Only its seventh part has survived, and it brings mentions of Svatopluk’s coronation, of his title of prince of princes and of his seat Džirváb.

children.text: The Book of Precious Records was written at the beginning of the 10th century, after 903. It is made up of several chapters, of which the seventh part brings us mentions of Svatopluk’s coronation, of his being titled prince of princes and of his seat Džirváb. It was written by the Arab-Persian geographer, traveller and encyclopaedist Abu ʿAli Ahmad ibn ʿUmar
He probably wrote it between the years

. In compiling the text the author probably drew, besides his own experience as a traveller, on the Kitáb al-masálik wa l-mamálik by Ibn Hurdádbih of 885, as well as on a lost book of the same name compiled before the year 900 by the Samanid vizier Abu Abdallah Muhammad al-Džajhání. The Book of Precious Records is an important source for our knowledge of the history of the early Slavs, above all of the Rus and the Croats. Only its 7th part has survived; it deals with geography and also contains information about the Bulgars, the Burtas, the Slavs, the Magyars, the Khazars and other peoples. It also mentions King Svatopluk (870–894). It gives the seat of King Svatopluk by the name of Džirváb. The translation of this name, evidently garbled in Arabic, is unclear. It may have been a corruption of the name Grad, from which some derive Veligrad. Equally, however, it may be a now-forgotten name of the hillfort at Mikulčice or of some other important hillfort. The exceptional character of this work lies above all in the fact that it was written by a contemporary of the Great Moravian Empire, who had, so to speak, information „from first hand“. It brings us a great many details and points of interest from the life of the Moravian Slavs. Among other things, it is worth noting that it gives Svatopluk the title „prince of princes“ and at the same time states that he was „crowned“. The work also gives the name Wáb-Nít, which in the past some authors (e.g. L. Havlík) interpreted as Nitra; at present, however, such a transcription of the Arabicised name and its translation is called into question, and J. Steinhübel, for example, considers it to be Kyiv.

blocks.text:
The Slavs
Between the land of the Pechenegs and the land of the Slavs there is a distance of ten days (of travel). On its frontier there is a town which is called Vá'b-Nít. You reach their country through steppes and trackless regions in which there are springs of water and dense forests. The lands of the Slavs are flat and wooded. There are their dwellings. They have neither vineyards nor tilled fields. They have certain wooden vessels in which there are openings for the bees and the honey, and they call them ulišče. From a single vessel ten ewers of honey can be taken. The Slavs pasture swine in the same way as sheep.
If one of them dies, they burn him. If a relative of their women dies, they wound their arms and faces with a knife. When they have burned a corpse somewhere, they come to the place of burning on the following day, gather up the ashes, lay them in an earthenware vessel and set the vessel on a raised place. When a year has passed since the death of the relative, they take with them some twenty vessels full of honey and go out with them to that raised place. And when they have all gathered there, they eat and drink. Then they return home. If the dead man had three wives and one of them believes that he loved her best, she takes two beams and sets them in the ground not far from the dead man. Across the beams she lays a third beam, fastens a rope to it, stands on a stool and ties the other end of the rope around her neck. When she has done this, they take the stool from under her and she is left hanging until she chokes and dies. Then they throw her into the fire and she burns. All the Slavs venerate fire.
They commonly sow millet. At harvest time they take some of the millet seed on a spoon, raise the spoon towards heaven and say: „Lord, thou art our provider, grant us a rich harvest!“ They have various musical instruments: lutes, tamburas and pipes. Their pipes are two cubits long and their lute has eight strings.
They make their drinks from honey. When they burn their dead, they play on musical instruments. They maintain that one should rejoice then, since God has received the departed into his mercy. They have few draught animals, and only men of standing own a horse. Their weapons are throwing spears, shields and lances. They have no others.
Their ruler is crowned. They obey him and act according to his commands. His seat is in the middle of the land of the Slavs. The most important and best known among them is the lord who holds the rank of prince of princes. They call him Svatopluk. He is more powerful than the župan, and the župan is his deputy. This ruler has many riding horses, and his dishes are prepared for him from mares’ milk. He has excellent, strong and precious armour, and the town in which he resides is called Džirváb. In this town a market is held for three days every month. At that time the Slavs conclude bargains among themselves and sell.
In their country the winter is harsh. For that reason they dig their dwellings beneath the ground, roof them with a wooden roof such as covers churches, and heap earth over it. A man enters such a dwelling with his family and brings in wood and a few stones. Then he lights a fire in it and keeps it burning until the stones glow red. When they are at their hottest, he pours water over them and the dwelling grows warm. Then they all take off their outer garments and remain in the dwelling the whole winter until spring.
Their ruler collects dues (taxes) from them every year. If someone has a daughter, he takes a garment from her clothes once a year. If someone has a son, he takes a garment from his clothes as well. If someone has neither daughter nor son, he takes a garment from the clothes of his wife or his concubine.
If a thief is caught in the kingdom of the Slavs, their ruler has him hanged or sends him to Džíra – the most distant province of his realm.
